We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts: 168.60, 143.85, 130.30, 22.80, 21.35, 19.20. Aromatic carbons typically appear around 110-160 ppm. Here we have three peaks in that region: 168.60 (maybe carbonyl), 143.85, 130.30. 168.6 could be carbonyl (C=O) not aromatic. Aromatic carbons are usually 110-160, but 168 is high for aromatic (maybe conjugated carbonyl). So likely aromatic carbons correspond to 143.85 and 130.30. That's 2 aromatic carbons. However could be more if the molecule has aromatic ring with multiple carbons but overlapping signals? The total number of carbons observed is 6 peaks. Could be a benzene ring (6 aromatic carbons) but we only see 2 aromatic peaks due to symmetry (e.g., para-disubstituted benzene gives 4 distinct aromatic carbons? Actually para-disubstituted benzene gives 4 distinct aromatic carbons: two sets of equivalent pairs. But we have only 2 aromatic peaks, maybe a highly symmetric like 1,3,5-trisubstituted? That gives 3 distinct aromatic carbons. Not 2. Could be 1,4-disubstituted (para) gives 4 distinct aromatic carbons (two pairs). So 2 peaks suggests maybe a fused aromatic system with symmetry? But we also have aliphatic peaks at 22.8,21.35,19.2 (three aliphatic carbons). So total carbons =6. So molecule has 6 carbons total. Aromatic carbons likely 2? That would give 4 aliphatic, but we have only 3 aliphatic peaks. So maybe one carbon is carbonyl (168.6) not aromatic, leaving 2 aromatic, 3 aliphatic, total 5? But we have 6 peaks, so carbonyl counts as one. So composition: carbonyl (C=O) 168.6, aromatic C 143.85, aromatic C 130.30, aliphatic C 22.8, 21.35, 19.2. That's 2 aromatic carbons.

Thus answer integer 2.
